newsitem.title: UK: IEA sees weaker oil prices despite robust demand.
newsitem.headline: IEA sees weaker oil prices despite robust demand.

text.p: Oil prices are set to fall later this year as stocks rise despite higher than expected demand due to strong U.S. gasoline consumption this spring, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Tuesday.
The Paris-based agency revised up its estimates of world oil demand for 1997 and 1998 by 100,000 barrels per day (bpd) to 73.8 million and 75.6 million bpd respectively.

Estimated demand in the second quarter of this year was revised up by 400,000 bpd to 72.6 million bpd due largely to robust U.S. gasoline demand and continued high growth rates in several Asian and Latin American developing countries, the IEA said in its monthly Oil Market Report.
Demand for crude from the Organisation of Petroleum

Exporting Countries (OPEC) was also revised up as a result -- by 600,000 bpd to 25.2 million in the second quarter and by 200,000 bpd to 25.7 million for 1997 as a whole -- but remained well below the group's average output.

"Despite continued year-on-year U.S.-led demand strength, oil markets in the second half of 1997 are expected to soften appreciably from the tighter than anticipated second quarter 1997," the West's energy watchdog said.

"Projections of world demand and non-OPEC supply for the remainder of the year suggest that there will be very substantial increases in inventories, unless OPEC crude oil output is reduced significantly," it said.

World oil inventories are estimated to have risen by 1.6 million bpd in the second quarter of 1997 as a seasonal demand decline of 1.4 million bpd was compounded by small increases in supply from non-OPEC producers and higher OPEC Natural Gas Liquids (NGL) production.

For the remainder of the year, demand growth and increases in non-OPEC supply of around two million bpd are expected to cancel each other out but the implied call for OPEC barrels will remain well below the group's current average output of 27 million bpd, assuming a resumption of Iraqi exports.
"The return of Iraqi crude to the export markets is the most important near-term wildcard for world oil supply," the IEA said.
Baghdad suspended exports of around 660,000 bpd in late May after reaching the $2 billion cash limit for the first 180 days of a United Nations oil-for-food deal.
The deal was renewed on June 8 but Iraqi authorities, unhappy with a cumbersome process for distributing aid, have delayed the resumption of exports.
The U.N. hopes to receive the revised Iraqi food distribution plan by 2000 GMT on Tuesday.
